newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Viacom, News Corp chase India youth.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Viacom, News Corp chase India youth.

text.p: U.S.-based Viacom Inc's MTV, after watching rival News Corp's Star TV unit steal ahead in a quest for the musical soul of India's huge youth market, has rolled out a plan to give more airtime to the local pop scene.
Television music channels MTV and Channel V, which is 50 percent owned by Star, are battling for position in a market which has still to take off, executives from both companies told Reuters.
"Eyes will glaze over when you ask for projections on the growth of the market. No-one knows," said Jules Fuller, the deputy general manager for Channel V in India.
"The potential is mega," Sudhanshu Sarronwala, general manager of MTV India Pvt Ltd said.
The six-month old MTV India is the latest baby of an 18-month-old partnership between MTV Networks and Polygram NV which already co-owns MTV Mandarin and MTV Asia.
It plans to show 16 hours a day of Indian programmes and the rest will be fed by MTV Asia, the channel currently on the air here.

Both Channel V and MTV India feed off the advertising revenues that their shows generate, but are just scratching the surface in a country where the total spending on television advertising is only $350 million annually.
But MTV India's business manager Sameer Aurora describes the growth in TV advertising spending in the past few years as exponential both in terms of money and brand proliferation.
Capturing the youth market in a population of 930 million is a big prize as the benefits of the economic liberalisation embarked upon five years ago are manifest in peoples' pockets.
So does Channel V have any projection beyond the short term for advertising revenues?
"No, just up," Fuller said, laughing.
News Corp chairman Rupert Murdoch will be watching that space closely, as the company has identified India as key to turning around the fortunes of loss-making Star.
Channel V is turned on in around 12 million households and estimates of actual viewers are over 20 million, Fuller said.
MTV counts an audience of around 5.5 million households.
Both channels recognise that tapping into the local talent is the way to reach the Indian teen and twenties market.
"India has a very strong local culture and it is very difficult to penetrate with just American music," said Rina Dasgupta, marketing manager at production company BMG Crescendo (India) Pvt ltd.
It may have the second largest population in the world, but India's music industry sales at under $350 million annually are only the 22nd largest in the world.
However, tape cassettes sell at 20 to 30 rupees apiece (60 to 90 cents) and the country is the world's biggest buyer of tapes in terms of units sold, revealing the musical appetite.
Enter Hindi pop, a melange of catchy western beat and Indian instrumentals and lyrics, albeit liberally spiced with English to produce the "Hinglish" hybrid commonly spoken in India.
The genre's big break came two years ago when the country went wild over local pop star Alisha Chinai's "Made in India", which sold around four million units legitimately and pirated.

Indian pop's share of the market is just five or six percent, but it is the fastest growing sector and the channels see a role in both staying apace of the evolving tastes and helping to form the budding youth culture.

"We're in the business of connecting with the Indian youth audience through music TV and creating an environment for the brands that are interested in the same market," Sunil Lulla, MTV India's creative general manager said.
"Using the Hindi word, MTV aims to be the 'dhadkan' -- the heartbeat -- of the youth," Lulla said.

But while MTV promotes its gameplan to provide an expanding showcase for Indian pop music, a number of people in the industry from artists to production companies reckon Channel V got there first, and MTV in the past has been too dependent on American music.
"Channel V Indianised itself," Remo Fernandes, an established star on India's pop circuit, told Reuters.
The Channel V package now boasts around 45 percent Hindi content, which is weighted at 65 percent in the peak viewing hours, he said.
"The whole thing is about aspirations to the west but with a local flavour. The youth here want the things coming out of the west but they don't want to be American," Channel V's Fuller said.
